title: Pour It
context: Grade 3, the first working topic on capacity. An adult sees a jug being filled, which a child can do at a tap. What is being settled is which unit fits which container, and how big a litre is: small vessels poured one after another reach the litre mark exactly, and half a litre and a quarter of a litre are the middle and the quarter of the jug. A child who has only met the word litre on a bottle will call every container a litre, and will say a bucket holds the same as a cup because both are full.

writeup.why: Choose millilitres or litres for a real container, pour small vessels into a one litre jug and read the level at a mark, find half a litre and a quarter of a litre, and sort real containers by whether they hold more or less than a litre.
writeup.look: A glass measuring jug with its marks at the left, a row of labelled standard vessels beside it, a shelf of real containers at the right, mL and L tags, a litre line across the table, and a pour counter at the top left of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Pour It' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many vessels have been poured into the measuring jug. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The glass measuring jug stands at x 120, y 230, 200 wide and 400 tall, with a near-black mark at every hundred millilitres from 0 at the bottom to one litre at the top, evenly spaced, the half way and quarter way marks a little longer and labelled in words, and each long mark carrying its unit. Water in the jug is clear blue-grey and rises to the new mark with a short ripple. The row of standard vessels stands on a table line at y 560 from x 360, each about 120 wide and drawn as a recognisable flat illustration with its capacity written on its side in digits and its unit: 50 mL, 100 mL, 200 mL, 500 mL and 1 L. The shelf of real containers runs along the right of the working area at x 620 to x 1100, y 230 and y 380 in two rows: a teacup, a mug, a bottle, a kettle, a pot, a bucket, a drum, a car fuel tank, a juice packet, a bowl of curd, a syringe and a spoon, each in its own natural colours. Two label tags, mL and L, hang at x 640, y 210 and x 780, y 210, each 120 by 50. The litre line is a long near-black line across the table at x 360 to x 1100, y 520, with a More side above it and a Less side below it, each labelled in words. A pan with a cup beside it stands at x 940, y 560 for the cups count. A deep blue tag beside the jug shows the reading taken, a green tag the amount reached, and a vermilion ring sits round the unit fact one litre and one thousand millilitres when the child drops a container on a tag. The pour counter sits in the count corner, the vessels poured so far. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing a count of vessels, the millilitres at a mark or the number of cups into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours, and the chapter's four roles are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate, labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag, labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from sit inside a vermilion ring, labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag, labelled Second or Left. Every ruler mark, scale mark and plain edge is near-black, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of the four, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a measure is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The measuring jug and the shelf show the last pouring, with the reading in a deep blue tag, the amount reached in a green tag, and the containers in their own colours.

phases.win: the container settles on its tag and the unit fact one litre beside one thousand millilitres lights in a vermilion ring

phases.goal: small amounts are measured in millilitres and large amounts in litres
phases.says: Pour some water in. Is this a small amount or a large amount?

writeup.delight: Two small surprises. On the second phase, as the last vessel is poured, the water climbs to the litre mark and stops with a tiny ripple, and the vessels lined up beside the jug light together like cups on a shelf. On the fourth phase, when the pan is filled cup by cup, each cup tips in with a splash and the level in the pan rises by one equal step every time.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet poured. On the first phase the glass jug stands empty at the left, a teacup, a bucket and a bottle wait on the shelf, and the mL and L tags hang over them. On the second the jug is empty with its marks showing and a row of vessels marked fifty, a hundred, two hundred and five hundred millilitres stands beside it. On the third the jug stands with its half way and quarter way marks labelled and a bowl of curd, a jug of water, a glass of buttermilk and a juice packet wait beside it. On the fourth a shelf of containers waits under a litre line with a More side and a Less side, and a pan and a cup stand to one side. One thing moves, once: the tap, or the first vessel on the second phase, gives one slow drip while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any container poured at the tap, any vessel poured into the jug in any order, the half way and quarter way marks, and the More and Less sides. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on a kettle, a syringe, a bucket, a pot, a bottle, a measuring jug, a glass of milk, a fuel tank, a spoon and a pan, each a real container.
voiceLines: A glass jug, some small vessels and a shelf of real containers. Let us pour.
Pour some water in. Is this a small amount or a large amount?
Pour the small vessels into the big jug. How many does it take to reach the top?
Pour to the middle mark. Which thing holds about as much?
Does this hold more than the jug, or less? Drag it to its side.
A new container. Is it a small amount or a large amount?
Free play. Pour any container, fill the jug your way, and sort what you like.
Look at the water again. Read the level at the nearest mark.
You poured, read the level at a mark, and sorted the containers against a litre.

observations.soWhat: half a litre is the middle of the jug and a quarter of a litre is a quarter of the way up.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a ruler, a measuring tape, a metre rod, a paper clip, a pencil, a book, a door, a ribbon, mangoes, a loaf of bread, potatoes, a bag of salt, a two pan balance with iron weights, a kitchen scale, measuring jugs, a glass, a teacup, a bucket, a bottle, a pot, a juice packet. The object is the thing the child measures, weighs or pours, and a plain bar or tank appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every scale is drawn with its marks evenly spaced and its zero at the edge: a ruler from 0, a metre rod in ten equal tens, a jug in equal marks, a balance with its beam level or tilted by the true difference. A reading is always taken at a mark, never between two.

Every unit is written next to its number, and a number is never written bare where a unit belongs. A unit fact is shown with both its sides, so 1 m = 100 cm is one object and one hundred centimetre marks side by side.

Converting is something the child does: a metre rod breaks into a hundred centimetre marks, a kilogram bag pours out a thousand gram dots, a litre jug empties into a thousand millilitre drops. The vermilion ring carries the times 100 or times 1000 step while it happens.
A sum or a difference is laid out in columns, units over their column, the second amount directly under the first, with a carried amount shown above the column it joins.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance. Large amounts are shown as a few tens, hundreds or thousands.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a mark or a reading the child is looking at, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a mango stays yellow and a metal weight stays dark grey. The four roles of the chapter are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate and is labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag and is labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from, such as one metre is one hundred centimetres, sit inside a vermilion ring and are labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag and are labelled Second or Left. Those four are the same four in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Every ruler mark, scale mark, outline and plain edge is near-black, and the stage still reads with the colour taken away because each role is named in writing first.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.

voice.onNext: A new container. Is it a small amount or a large amount?

voice.onFinish: You poured, read the level at a mark, and sorted the containers against a litre.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Pour any container, fill the jug your way, and sort what you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.

phase_map.concept: Standard vessels: from 50 mL up to 1 L
Half a litre and a quarter of a litre
More than or less than one litre

placement.where: After the class has poured a litre bottle of water into cups and a bowl by hand, and said which holds more. The tool is what lets a bucket and a teacup be poured against the same litre line, and what stops the pouring at the litre mark exactly, which a bottle and a cup cannot show in front of the child.

answer_key.rule: Capacity is how much liquid a container can hold. Small amounts are measured in millilitres and large amounts in litres, and one litre is one thousand millilitres. Small vessels poured into a one litre jug reach the litre mark exactly when their amounts add up to one litre: ten of one hundred millilitres, five of two hundred, two of five hundred. A level is read at a mark, never between two. Half a litre is five hundred millilitres and a quarter of a litre is two hundred and fifty millilitres, and a bowl of curd, a jug of water, a glass of buttermilk and a juice packet are only about those amounts. A bucket and a drum hold more than a litre, and a spoon and a teacup hold less.
answer_key.wrong: The measuring jug is emptied and poured again one vessel at a time, with the level read aloud at each mark, and the container is set beside the litre line so the child sees it hold more or less. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A cup holds a small amount of tea.
Small amounts are measured in millilitres.
One litre is one thousand millilitres, much more than a cup holds.
items.question: A cup of tea is measured. Which unit fits the capacity of the cup, millilitres or litres?
items.checkpoint: Small amounts are millilitres and large amounts are litres.
items.misconception: Choosing litres because litre is the word used for drinks.

steps: One litre is one thousand millilitres.
One small vessel holds five hundred millilitres, which is half of the jug.
So two vessels fill the jug.
items.question: A glass jug holds one litre. A small vessel holds five hundred millilitres. How many of the small vessels fill the jug?
items.checkpoint: Count how many small vessels make one litre.
items.misconception: Saying five hundred, the number on the vessel, instead of how many vessels.

steps: One litre is one thousand millilitres.
The half way mark is half of the bottle.
Half of one thousand is five hundred.
So the bottle holds five hundred millilitres, which is half a litre.
items.question: A bottle is marked up to one litre. Water is poured to the half way mark. How many millilitres of water are in the bottle?
items.checkpoint: Half a litre is half of one thousand millilitres.
items.misconception: Giving one hundred millilitres, a guess, because half of a litre was not worked out.

steps: A cup holds a small amount, much less than one litre.
A drum is much bigger than a one litre jug.
So the drum holds more than one litre.
items.question: A drum and a cup are both filled with water. Which one holds more than one litre?
items.checkpoint: Compare each container with the one litre jug.
items.misconception: Saying the cup, because a cup feels full and the drum is only a picture.

items.question: A kettle is filled at a tap. Which unit fits its capacity, millilitres or litres?
items.final_answer: Litres, because a kettle holds a large amount of water

items.question: A pot holds one litre of water. It is poured into small cups that each hold two hundred millilitres. How many cups does it fill?
items.final_answer: Five cups, because five cups of two hundred millilitres make one litre

items.question: A one litre water bottle is filled to the half way mark. Is the water about a quarter of a litre, half a litre or one litre?
items.final_answer: Half a litre, because the bottle is half full

items.question: A car fuel tank and a spoon are filled with water. Which one holds less than one litre?
items.final_answer: The spoon, because a spoon holds only a very small amount

items.question: A syringe and a bucket are both filled with water. Which one is measured in millilitres and which in litres?
items.final_answer: The syringe in millilitres and the bucket in litres

items.question: A small measuring jug is marked every 20 mL. The water reaches the seventh mark above 0. How many millilitres of water are in the jug?
items.final_answer: 140 mL, because seven marks of 20 mL each give 140 mL

items.question: A glass of milk holds about a quarter of a litre. About how many such glasses fill a one litre jug?
items.final_answer: About four glasses, because four quarters make one litre

items.question: A cup holds 140 mL of water. How many cups fill a pan that holds 560 mL?
items.final_answer: 4 cups, because counting 140, 280, 420, 560 takes four steps

student_controls.effect: pours water into a container or the measuring jug, and the level rises to the next mark
tapping one pours it into the measuring jug and adds one to the pour counter
dropping a container on one chooses the unit for its capacity
tapping one pours the jug to that mark and sets real things beside it
student_controls.control: Half way and quarter way marks

student_controls.effect: dropping a container on one sorts it against the one litre line
types a count of vessels or an amount in millilitres

teaching_notes: Pour real water before the tool opens: a litre bottle into small cups, then into a bowl, and say which container held more. Let a teacup and a bucket stand beside the litre bottle so the class can see a bucket hold more and a teacup hold less. Millilitres are for small amounts and litres for large ones, and one litre is one thousand millilitres. When the class pours small cups into the litre bottle, ask them to count the pours before the water reaches the top, and read the level at a mark, never between two marks. Say about whenever a bowl of curd, a jug of water, a glass of buttermilk or a juice packet is set beside half a litre or a quarter of a litre: they are about those amounts, never exactly. Do not ask for the exact capacity of a thing. Use fresh numbers: the exercise's seven containers and its cup problem are the child's to try.
generation_prompt: Build a pouring tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, drawn from real everyday objects as recognisable flat illustrations in their own natural colours, with no photographs and no people. A clear glass measuring jug, 200 wide and 400 tall, stands at the left of the working area with an evenly spaced near-black mark at every hundred millilitres from 0 up to one litre, the half way and quarter way marks longer and labelled. Beside it stands a row of standard vessels, each with its capacity written on it: 50 mL, 100 mL, 200 mL, 500 mL and 1 L. A shelf at the right holds real containers to choose from: a teacup, a mug, a bottle, a kettle, a pot, a bucket, a drum, a car fuel tank, a juice packet, a bowl of curd, a syringe and a spoon. A tap pours water, and tapping a vessel pours it into the measuring jug so the water rises to the new mark. A pour counter at the top left of the canvas counts the vessels poured. Two label tags, mL and L, hang over the shelf: dropping a container on one chooses its unit. A line across the table marks one litre with a More side and a Less side for sorting containers. A deep blue tag shows the reading taken, a green tag the amount reached, and a vermilion ring marks the unit fact one litre and one thousand millilitres. A number pad types a count of vessels or an amount in millilitres. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Pour water into a container. Drop it on mL or L. Then pour small vessels into the one litre jug and count them.
